Explanation: These four muscles (SITS) form the rotator cuff and stabilize the glenohumeral joint; teres major is not a cuff muscle and is correctly excluded.
Source Section: Shoulder & Elbow / Shoulder anatomy; PDF pp. 116
Notes: Verified against standard anatomy (Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy). No competing 4-member category.

Explanation: The four principal spondyloarthritis entities; enthesitis and axial or peripheral inflammation are characteristic. HLA-B27 strength varies by disease and phenotype and is not universal.
Source Section: Seronegative Spondyloarthritis / Overview; PDF pp. 45-49
Notes: Preserve qualifier: not all patients are HLA-B27 positive. Board overlap: individual members may collide with HLA-B27 or enthesitis categories.

Explanation: These enteric bacteria can precede sterile reactive arthritis; organisms do not infect the joint. Chlamydia (genitourinary) is the classic non-enteric trigger and is correctly excluded here.
Source Section: Seronegative Spondyloarthritis / Reactive arthritis; PDF pp. 49
Notes: Classic enteric four; not exhaustive (C. difficile also reported). Keep 'enteric' qualifier in title to exclude Chlamydia.

Explanation: These agents can raise serum urate and contribute to gout risk. The aspirin effect is dose-dependent: low-dose (<=2 g/day) raises urate while high-dose (>3 g/day) is uricosuric, so the tile specifies low-dose aspirin.
Source Section: Non-Rheumatologic Diseases / Gout; PDF pp. 11
Notes: Low-dose qualifier is required and verified (Leung et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2022, PMID 35787862; Neogi, NEJM 2011, DOI 10.1056/NEJMcp1001124). Epidemiologic signal is inconsistent (NHANES, PMID 37282368) but mechanism is established. Many other drugs also qualify (cyclosporine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) - potential board overlap.

Explanation: Cartilage degeneration with adjacent bone remodeling produces this characteristic radiographic cluster. Findings are supportive rather than individually specific.
Source Section: Non-Rheumatologic Diseases / Osteoarthritis; PDF pp. 10
Notes: Verified (Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease). Contrast with RA's uniform joint-space loss and erosions for board separation.

Tile 4: Blue when aligned parallel to the compensator
Explanation: CPP crystals are typically rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent; under a compensator they appear blue when aligned parallel to its slow axis. Cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) supports CPPD but can be absent and is not specific.
Source Section: Non-Rheumatologic Diseases / CPPD; PDF pp. 12
Notes: CAUTION/board overlap: 'weak positive birefringence' and 'blue parallel to compensator' are closely related optical descriptors (one is the property, one its microscopic manifestation). They are retained as distinct tiles but should not both appear on a 16-tile board as if independent. Color requires compensated polarized microscopy and correct orientation.

Explanation: Defective osteoclast resorption yields dense brittle bone (fractures), narrowed cranial foramina (cranial nerve compression), and loss of marrow space (pancytopenia with compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis). Severity varies markedly by genetic form.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Consequences of osteopetrosis; Marble bone disease sequelae
Source Section: Non-Rheumatologic Diseases / Osteopetrosis; PDF pp. 16
Notes: Preserve qualifier: possible, not universal findings; manifestations differ between infantile (malignant) and adult (benign) forms.

Explanation: Poor mineralization of growing bone causes metaphyseal cupping/fraying, prominent costochondral junctions (rachitic rosary), and soft skull bones (craniotabes).
Source Section: Non-Rheumatologic Diseases / Osteomalacia-Rickets; PDF pp. 17
Notes: Verified (Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics). Findings not individually diagnostic; craniotabes has other causes (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta, normal newborns).

Explanation: Skull/bone enlargement increases hat size and can cause hearing loss; extensive hypervascular pagetic bone can contribute to high-output failure, and sarcomatous transformation (osteosarcoma) is a rare late complication.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Paget disease (osteitis deformans) manifestations and complications
Source Section: Non-Rheumatologic Diseases / Osteitis deformans; PDF pp. 18
Notes: Preserve qualifier: high-output failure and osteosarcoma are uncommon; hearing loss is multifactorial (ossicular and nerve mechanisms).

Connection Title: Conventional synthetic DMARDs used in RA
Explanation: These conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are used in rheumatoid arthritis and are distinct from symptomatic NSAIDs and from biologic/targeted-synthetic DMARDs.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Rheumatoid arthritis; PDF pp. 27
Notes: Verified (ACR RA treatment guideline). Clean class; distinguish from bDMARDs (anti-TNF) and tsDMARDs (JAK inhibitors) on a board.

Connection Title: Medications classically linked to drug-induced lupus
Explanation: These drugs can cause a lupus-like syndrome; risk is highest with procainamide and hydralazine. Anti-histone antibodies are typical but not uniquely diagnostic.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / SLE, Drug-induced lupus; PDF pp. 28
Notes: Preserve qualifier: risk differs substantially by drug. Other culprits (minocycline, quinidine, anti-TNF agents) also qualify - potential board overlap.

Explanation: Transplacental maternal anti-Ro/SSA (and sometimes anti-La/SSB) antibodies can produce neonatal cardiac (congenital heart block), cutaneous, hematologic, or hepatic involvement. Not every exposed infant is affected.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / SLE; PDF pp. 28
Notes: Preserve qualifier: possible findings, not universal. Congenital AV block is the one typically permanent manifestation; others are usually transient.

Explanation: Autoimmune exocrine-gland injury produces dry eyes and mouth, reduced tear production, and focal lymphocytic sialadenitis on minor salivary gland biopsy.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Sjogren syndrome; PDF pp. 29
Notes: Preserve qualifier: symptoms and Schirmer alone are nonspecific; biopsy graded by focus score per ACR/EULAR 2016 criteria.

Explanation: APS is characterized by venous and arterial thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity; livedo reticularis is a common associated cutaneous finding. Diagnosis requires persistent antiphospholipid antibodies plus clinical criteria.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Antiphospholipid syndrome; PDF pp. 30
Notes: Preserve qualifier: no single clue is diagnostic; requires persistently positive lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, or anti-beta2-glycoprotein I.

Explanation: These are distinct cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis: heliotrope eyelid rash, Gottron papules over the knuckles, the shawl sign (posterior shoulders/upper back), and the V-sign (anterior neck/chest). Each is a different anatomic distribution.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Polymyositis-Dermatomyositis; PDF pp. 33
Notes: Verified. Shawl and V signs are distinct distributions, not synonyms. Mechanic's hands intentionally omitted (more specific to antisynthetase syndrome).

Explanation: Four components of the classic CREST phenotype of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Esophageal dysmotility is the fifth (omitted) component; not all features need be present simultaneously.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: CREST features; Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Scleroderma; PDF pp. 37
Notes: Preserve qualifier: this is 4 of 5 CREST components (E = esophageal dysmotility omitted). Associated with anti-centromere antibody. Board note: do not place esophageal dysmotility as a distractor on the same board.

Explanation: These findings support sarcoidosis after exclusion of other granulomatous disorders. Serum ACE and the elevated bronchoalveolar lavage CD4:CD8 ratio have limited sensitivity and specificity and are not required.
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Sarcoidosis; PDF pp. 38
Notes: Preserve qualifier: noncaseating granulomas have many causes; sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion. Classified under Pathology though commonly multisystem/pulmonary.

Explanation: Abnormal bone remodeling (Paget), prior radiation, and inherited tumor-suppressor defects (germline RB1 in hereditary retinoblastoma; TP53 in Li-Fraumeni) are established osteosarcoma risk contexts.
Source Section: Primary Bone Tumors / Osteosarcoma; PDF pp. 57
Notes: Verified. 'Hereditary retinoblastoma' qualifier preserves the germline RB1 risk context (secondary osteosarcoma risk, radiation-independent).

Explanation: Ewing sarcoma often arises in the diaphysis of long bones and shows a lamellated 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction, small round blue cell histology, and the t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 fusion in most cases.
Source Section: Primary Bone Tumors / Ewing sarcoma; PDF pp. 59
Notes: Preserve qualifier: other sites and fusion partners (e.g., EWSR1-ERG) occur; histology/periosteal appearance are not individually specific. Board overlap: small round blue cell tumor differential.

Explanation: In an older patient, cranial ischemic symptoms with compatible temporal artery histology support GCA; visual symptoms warrant urgent high-dose glucocorticoids. Biopsy can miss skip lesions.
Source Section: Vasculitides / Giant cell arteritis; PDF pp. 69
Notes: Preserve qualifier: biopsy skip lesions occur and giant cells are not required in every positive specimen. Strong link to polymyalgia rheumatica (board overlap).

Explanation: The upper-airway, pulmonary, renal, and PR3-ANCA pattern is characteristic of GPA. PR3-ANCA is not universal and renal involvement or cavitation may be absent.
Source Section: Vasculitides / GPA; PDF pp. 77
Notes: Preserve qualifier: ~10-20% PR3-ANCA negative. Board overlap with MPA and EGPA (ANCA-associated vasculitides); the sinus + cavitation combination distinguishes GPA.

Explanation: IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis affects skin, joints, gut, and kidney, classically in children after an upper respiratory infection. The tetrad need not occur simultaneously; renal involvement may appear later.
Source Section: Vasculitides / IgA vasculitis; PDF pp. 78
Notes: Verified. Mandatory feature is palpable purpura; renal manifestation (IgA nephropathy-type) may be delayed.

Connection Title: Autoimmune rheumatic diseases associated with Raynaud phenomenon
Explanation: Each connective tissue disease is associated with secondary Raynaud phenomenon, though frequency and significance differ (near-universal in systemic sclerosis and MCTD, less so in SLE and Sjogren).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Connective tissue diseases with secondary Raynaud
Source Section: Rheumatologic Diseases / Sjogren, Raynaud, Scleroderma-MCTD; PDF pp. 29,36-37
Notes: Preserve qualifier: association strength varies widely. Board overlap: these four also cluster under 'ANA-positive connective tissue diseases.'

Explanation: These fracture and entrapment sites threaten the ulnar nerve at the wrist (hook of hamate, Guyon canal) or elbow (medial epicondyle, cubital tunnel). Deficits vary by level; dorsal hand sensation is usually spared in Guyon canal lesions.
Source Section: Brachial Plexus / Ulnar nerve; PDF pp. 103
Notes: Verified. Preserve level-dependent deficit nuance for teaching.

Connection Title: Muscles supplied by the obturator nerve
Explanation: The obturator nerve supplies these medial-thigh adductors. Adductor magnus is dually innervated; only its adductor part is obturator-supplied (the hamstring part is tibial-division sciatic), so that tile is qualified.
Source Section: Lower Extremity Nerves / Obturator nerve; PDF pp. 142
Notes: Qualifier on adductor magnus verified (Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy). Board note: obturator externus and (variably) pectineus are also obturator-innervated - avoid using them as distractors on the same board.

Explanation: Gluteus maximus and the three hamstrings shown extend the hip. The short head of biceps femoris does not cross the hip and is correctly excluded; the long-head qualifier prevents that objection.
Source Section: Hip & Knee / Hip anatomy; Lower Extremity Nerves; PDF pp. 144,153
Notes: Long-head qualifier verified. Board note: the adductor (hamstring) part of adductor magnus is also a hip extensor - a plausible competing member; avoid on the same board.

Connection Title: Quadriceps muscles that extend the knee
Explanation: These four femoral-nerve-innervated muscles form the quadriceps femoris and act through the extensor mechanism to extend the knee.
Source Section: Hip & Knee / Knee anatomy; PDF pp. 160
Notes: Verified. Clean closed set; only rectus femoris also crosses the hip (a teaching nuance, not a competing member).

Connection Title: Principal stabilizing ligaments of the knee
Explanation: The cruciate ligaments resist anteroposterior tibial translation and the collateral ligaments resist valgus (MCL) and varus (LCL) stress.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: ACL PCL MCL LCL; Cruciate and collateral knee ligaments
Source Section: Hip & Knee / Knee anatomy and ligament injuries; PDF pp. 160-162
Notes: Verified. Clean canonical four-ligament set.

Connection Title: Pediatric hip disorders that can present with referred knee pain
Explanation: Hip pathology commonly refers pain to the thigh or knee via the obturator nerve, so knee symptoms warrant hip examination. SCFE presents with knee or distal-thigh pain in roughly a quarter of cases, and Legg-Calve-Perthes classically refers pain to the knee.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hip pathology presenting as knee pain
Source Section: Childhood MSK / SCFE, Perthes; Hip & Knee / Dislocation; PDF pp. 157,185-187
Notes: REVISED: original tile 'Developmental hip dysplasia' replaced with 'Transient synovitis of the hip.' Infant DDH is clinically silent/painless and is detected by Ortolani/limited abduction, not knee pain (AAP DDH clinical report, Shaw & Segal, Pediatrics 2016; Singh et al., JAMA 2024 Rational Clinical Examination). Referred knee pain is best documented for SCFE (Webb et al., Am Fam Physician 2025; Karkenny et al., Pediatrics in Review 2018) and Perthes; transient synovitis is a common pediatric hip condition that presents with hip/limp and thigh-knee discomfort (de Borja et al., Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2022). Board note: referred knee pain is strongest for SCFE and Perthes; hip dislocation fits the general referred-pain principle but is less distinctive.

Explanation: These settings compromise bone perfusion or marrow microcirculation and predispose to avascular (osteo)necrosis, classically of the femoral head. They do not invariably cause osteonecrosis.
Source Section: Hip & Knee / Avascular necrosis; PDF pp. 159
Notes: Verified. 'Heavy' alcohol qualifier preserves the dose-related risk context.

Connection Title: Causes of acute limb compartment syndrome
Explanation: These processes raise pressure within a closed fascial compartment, compromising perfusion and injuring nerve and muscle. Risk depends on severity; palpable pulses do not exclude the diagnosis.
Source Section: Hip & Knee / Limb compartment syndrome; PDF pp. 164
Notes: Verified. Preserve nuance: normal pulses do not rule out compartment syndrome; fracture is the most common cause.

Connection Title: Bony tenderness sites in the Ottawa ankle-foot rules
Tile 1: Posterior edge or tip of lateral malleolus
Tile 2: Posterior edge or tip of medial malleolus
Explanation: These are the bony tenderness landmarks of the Ottawa ankle (malleolar) and foot (midfoot) rules, applied together with inability to bear weight for four steps. They are landmarks, not the complete rule.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Ottawa ankle and foot rule landmarks
Source Section: Foot & Ankle / Ankle sprain; PDF pp. 173
Notes: Verified against Ottawa Ankle Rules (Stiell et al.). Board note: apply with the weight-bearing criterion and age/exclusion caveats; tiles are landmarks only.

Tile 1: Tension (superolateral) side of the femoral neck
Explanation: Stress fractures at these sites carry high risk of displacement, nonunion, or avascular necrosis and need location-specific, often surgical, management. The tension-side femoral neck and the anterior tibial cortex ('dreaded black line') are classic high-risk tension-sided lesions.
Source Section: Foot & Ankle / Stress fractures; PDF pp. 176
Notes: Tension-side and anterior-cortex qualifiers verified (sports-medicine references, e.g., Boden & Osbahr). Board overlap: navicular and sesamoids are additional high-risk sites - avoid as distractors.

Explanation: These conventional NSAIDs reversibly inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce prostaglandin synthesis; aspirin is the exception (irreversible COX acetylation) and is correctly excluded.
Source Section: Pharmacology / Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories; PDF pp. 198
Notes: Verified (Goodman & Gilman). Clean mechanism-based set with aspirin as the deliberate contrast.

Explanation: Allopurinol and febuxostat reduce urate production (xanthine oxidase inhibition), probenecid is uricosuric, and pegloticase is a recombinant uricase. They are urate-lowering, not acute flare-relief, agents; pegloticase is reserved for refractory disease.
Source Section: Pharmacology / Gout medications; PDF pp. 200
Notes: Verified (ACR 2020 gout guideline). Preserve distinction from anti-inflammatory flare therapy (colchicine, NSAIDs, glucocorticoids).

Explanation: These nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates bind bone mineral and inhibit osteoclast-mediated resorption. Route and fracture-prevention evidence differ by agent.
Source Section: Pharmacology / Bisphosphonates; PDF pp. 201
Notes: Verified. Preserve qualifier: do not imply identical dosing, route, or fracture-prevention evidence (e.g., zoledronic acid IV; ibandronate has weaker non-vertebral fracture data).

Explanation: These four agents all bind TNF-alpha: adalimumab, infliximab, and golimumab are full-length monoclonal IgG antibodies and certolizumab pegol is a PEGylated Fab fragment. Etanercept (a TNFR2-Fc fusion protein) is correctly excluded.
Source Section: Pharmacology / TNF-alpha inhibitors; PDF pp. 203
Notes: Corrected mechanism wording: these antibodies bind TNF-alpha (ligand), not the TNF receptor (Pedersen & Maksymowych, Drugs 2018; AAP biosimilar technical report 2026). Certolizumab is a Fab fragment, not a full-length antibody - keep that qualifier.

Explanation: These prostanoids arise through the cyclooxygenase branch of arachidonic acid metabolism, in contrast to leukotrienes from the 5-lipoxygenase branch.
Source Section: Pharmacology / Arachidonic acid pathway; PDF pp. 195
Notes: Verified (Lippincott Biochemistry). Clean set; leukotrienes are the intended contrast.

Explanation: Volatile anesthetic/succinylcholine-triggered RYR1-mediated skeletal-muscle calcium release causes hypermetabolism and muscle injury, raising CO2 (hypercapnia) and lactate (lactic acidosis) and releasing intracellular potassium (hyperkalemia) and myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis).
Source Section: Skeletal Muscle / Malignant hyperthermia; PDF pp. 4
Notes: Preserve qualifier: these abnormalities are not unique to MH; rising end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign, and hyperthermia may be a late feature.
